desc:
Every subset of nums (chosen by position, so there are exactly 2n of them, the empty subset included) has a sum. Count the subsets whose sum is at most budget.

All elements are non-negative. Equal values at different positions count as different choices. The answer fits in a 32-bit integer because n ≤ 30.
hints: Trying every subset takes 2<sup>30</sup> steps, which is far too slow. Split the array into two halves.
Every subset is a pair: one subset of the left half and one of the right half. Each half has at most 2<sup>15</sup> subset sums, which you can list and sort.
For each left sum a, count the right sums that are at most budget - a. With both lists sorted, move one pointer down while the other goes up, or use binary search.
editorial: This is meet in the middle. Generate all subset sums of the first half L and of the second half R (at most 32,768 each, built by the usual doubling loop) and sort them. A whole subset has sum a + b with a from L and b from R, and every combination of an a and a b is a different subset, so we need the number of pairs with a + b ≤ budget.

Process L in increasing order while a pointer j into the sorted R only moves down: for a larger a the limit budget - a is smaller, so the count of admissible b values never grows. Add j (the number of right sums within the limit) for each a, and stop once a alone exceeds the budget. Sorting dominates, so the time is O(2n/2 · n) instead of O(2n).
